subChunks.title: Deadlocks, SELECT FOR UPDATE, and Advisory Locks
subChunks.hookHtml: Two transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds — deadlock. Understanding when deadlocks happen and how to prevent them is essential for reliable concurrent systems.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What is a deadlock

Transaction A holds lock on row X, wants lock on row Y. Transaction B holds lock on row Y, wants lock on row X. Both wait forever — the database detects this cycle and kills one transaction with an error.

SELECT FOR UPDATE — explicit row lock

BEGIN;
-- Lock Alice's row for update (others block on this row):
SELECT xp FROM apprentices WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
-- Now read and update safely:
UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 100 WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;

FOR UPDATE acquires a row-level exclusive lock. Other transactions that try to SELECT FOR UPDATE the same row will wait until the first transaction commits.

SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED

-- Process one unprocessed job without blocking:
SELECT id, payload FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY created_at
LIMIT 1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

SKIP LOCKED is the basis of queue-like patterns in PostgreSQL — multiple workers each grab a different row without waiting.

Preventing deadlocks

  1. Consistent lock ordering — always acquire locks on rows in the same order (e.g. always lock lower id first). Deadlocks cannot form if all transactions acquire locks in the same sequence.
  2. Keep transactions short — the longer a transaction holds locks, the more likely a deadlock.
  3. Lock at the start — acquire all needed locks at the beginning of the transaction.

Advisory locks

-- Application-level named lock:
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(12345);  -- waits until acquired
SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(12345);  -- returns false if unavailable

storyBeats.text: Two processes try to award the same badge simultaneously. One must wait. If they each hold half of what the other needs, neither can proceed.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: The cure for deadlocks is consistency. If every transaction acquires locks in the same order — always lock the lower apprentice ID first — no cycle can form. SELECT FOR UPDATE is your explicit lock request. SKIP LOCKED turns the table into a work queue.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Deadlock prevention analysis

Two transactions run concurrently:

-- Transaction A:
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE; -- locks id=1
SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE id = 2 FOR UPDATE; -- waits for B
...

-- Transaction B:
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE id = 2 FOR UPDATE; -- locks id=2
SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE; -- waits for A
...

Explain: (1) why this deadlocks, (2) how to fix it.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Why it deadlocks:
Transaction A holds a lock on id=1 and is waiting for id=2.
Transaction B holds a lock on id=2 and is waiting for id=1.
Neither can proceed — classic circular wait. PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one transaction with 'ERROR: deadlock detected'.

(2) Fix — consistent lock ordering:
Always lock the lower id first:

Transaction A AND Transaction B both:
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE; -- lower id first
SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE id = 2 FOR UPDATE;
...
COMMIT;

Now: when B tries to lock id=1, it waits for A to release it. A completes, then B proceeds. No deadlock — there is no circular dependency.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Write a query using SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED that would be used by a background worker to process one pending job from a jobs(id, payload, status) table without blocking other workers.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
BEGIN;

-- Grab one pending job that no other worker has locked:
SELECT id, payload
FROM   jobs
WHERE  status = 'pending'
ORDER BY id  -- consistent ordering helps avoid deadlocks across workers
LIMIT  1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

-- If a row was returned: process it, then:
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'processing' WHERE id = :returned_id;

COMMIT;

-- Why SKIP LOCKED: multiple workers can run concurrently.
-- Each grabs a different row (locked rows are skipped).
-- Without SKIP LOCKED, all workers would queue on the same row.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a deadlock is using a concrete example, and describe the consistent lock ordering strategy that prevents them.

options: Two or more transactions each waiting for a lock held by the other — creating a circular wait that can never resolve
A transaction that has been running for too long
A table lock that blocks all reads
A query that returns no rows due to conflicting WHERE conditions
questions.answer: Two or more transactions each waiting for a lock held by the other — creating a circular wait that can never resolve
questions.explanation: Deadlock is a circular dependency: A waits for B's lock; B waits for A's lock. The database detects this and kills one transaction to break the cycle.

options: Acquires a row-level exclusive lock — other FOR UPDATE transactions on the same row must wait
Marks the row as read-only until the transaction commits
Immediately updates the row to the specified values
Creates a snapshot of the row for the transaction's duration
questions.answer: Acquires a row-level exclusive lock — other FOR UPDATE transactions on the same row must wait
questions.explanation: FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows for the transaction's duration. Other transactions attempting SELECT FOR UPDATE on the same rows will block until the first transaction commits or rolls back.

questions.prompt: What does SKIP LOCKED do in `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`?
options: Skips rows that are already locked by other transactions — returns only unlocked rows
Skips the lock acquisition — reads without locking
Returns NULL for locked rows instead of waiting
Raises an error if any rows are locked
questions.answer: Skips rows that are already locked by other transactions — returns only unlocked rows
questions.explanation: SKIP LOCKED makes the query non-blocking: instead of waiting for locked rows, it simply skips them and returns other unlocked rows. This is the foundation of concurrent queue-worker patterns.

questions.prompt: Why does consistent lock ordering prevent deadlocks?
options: If all transactions acquire locks in the same order, circular dependencies cannot form — A always gets lock 1 before lock 2, so A never holds lock 2 while waiting for lock 1
Consistent ordering prevents any locking at all
Consistent ordering reduces the number of lock requests
Consistent ordering is enforced by the database automatically
questions.answer: If all transactions acquire locks in the same order, circular dependencies cannot form — A always gets lock 1 before lock 2, so A never holds lock 2 while waiting for lock 1
questions.explanation: A deadlock requires a cycle: A→B→A. If all transactions acquire locks in ascending ID order, A always holds lower IDs first. B can only be waiting for a lower ID, which it can get after A releases — no cycle can form.
